name: Clarito
description: The Argentine Martini: gin and dry vermouth, stirred hard, served brutally cold with a lemon twist. Older than most people assume.
funFact: Buenos Aires had a serious cocktail culture by the 1920s, and the Clarito — 'the clear little one' — was its house drink, poured in the grand cafés of Avenida de Mayo.

steps: Chill a coupe thoroughly in the freezer.
Stir the gin, vermouth and bitters over plenty of ice for 30 seconds.
Strain into the frozen coupe.
Express a wide lemon twist over the surface and rest it on the rim.

name: Gancia Batido
description: Gancia, lemon and sugar shaken to a foam — the Argentine aperitivo that college towns adopted and never gave back.
funFact: Gancia is an Italian bitter aperitif that found a second life in Argentina; batido versions are so entrenched that the brand is now more associated with Rosario than with Piedmont.

steps: Add the Gancia, lemon juice and sugar to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 15 seconds until foamy.
Pour unstrained into a rocks glass.
Top with a splash of soda and a lemon wheel.

name: Chuflay
description: Singani and ginger ale with a squeeze of lime — Bolivia's national highball, invented by homesick railway engineers.
funFact: The name is said to come from British railway workers asking for a 'short fly' — a quick drink — which Bolivian ears rendered as 'chuflay'. Singani is Bolivia's protected grape brandy.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the singani and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger ale.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Yungueñito
description: Singani shaken with fresh orange juice — the Yungas valleys in a glass, where Bolivia's oranges and its grape brandy come from the same slopes.
funFact: Named for Los Yungas, the humid valleys northeast of La Paz; the full-size version, the Yungueño, is served in a jug for the table.

steps: Add the singani, orange juice and syrup to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe or over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with an orange wheel.

name: Batida de Coco
description: Cachaça blended with coconut milk and condensed milk until it drinks like a cold dessert. Brazil's beach cocktail when the Caipirinha feels too sharp.
funFact: 'Batida' simply means 'beaten' or 'shaken' — the family covers dozens of fruit versions (maracujá, morango, amendoim), of which coconut is the one that travelled.

steps: Add the cachaça, coconut milk and condensed milk to a blender.
Add the ice and blend until smooth and frothy.
Pour into a chilled rocks glass.
Grate a little fresh coconut or dust cinnamon over the top.

name: Caipiroska
description: The Caipirinha with vodka instead of cachaça — cleaner, less funky, and the version most of the world actually orders.
funFact: Brazilian bars will make it without comment but consider it a compromise; the same swap with white rum is a Caipirissima, and with sake a Sakerinha.

steps: Put the lime wedges and sugar in the bottom of a sturdy rocks glass.
Muddle firmly until the sugar dissolves into the lime juice and oil.
Fill the glass with ice.
Pour over the vodka and stir hard from the bottom up.
Serve with the spent lime wedges still in the glass.

name: Capeta
description: 'Little devil': cachaça, guaraná powder, condensed milk and cinnamon — a Brazilian student drink built to keep you upright until sunrise.
funFact: Guaraná seed carries roughly twice the caffeine of coffee by weight, which is exactly the point — the Capeta is northeastern Brazil's original energy cocktail, decades before Red Bull.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a blender with the ice.
Blend on high until completely smooth.
Pour into a rocks glass.
Dust with extra cinnamon and serve cold.

name: Leite de Onça
description: 'Jaguar's milk': cachaça, condensed milk, cocoa and crème de cacao, shaken cold. Minas Gerais' answer to a nightcap.
funFact: A Festa Junina staple in Minas Gerais alongside quentão, and one of the few Brazilian drinks that is genuinely better made the night before and left in the fridge.

steps: Whisk the cocoa powder into a little of the warm milk to make a smooth paste, then cool.
Add the paste, remaining milk, condensed milk, crème de cacao and cachaça to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled tumbler.
Dust with cocoa powder or cinnamon.

name: Quentão
description: Festa Junina in a mug: cachaça simmered with ginger, cinnamon and citrus peel until the whole street smells like winter, in the middle of a Brazilian June.
funFact: Quentão means 'big hot one' and belongs to Festa Junina, the June harvest festivals — held in the Brazilian winter, which is why a country famous for cold drinks has a national mulled one.

steps: Melt the sugar in a heavy pan over medium heat until it just turns amber.
Add the ginger, cinnamon, cloves and orange peel and stir for a minute.
Pour in the water and simmer for 10 minutes to build the infusion.
Add the cachaça and heat gently — do not let it boil hard or you lose the alcohol.
Strain into mugs and serve steaming.
recipe.garnish: A cinnamon stick and a strip of orange peel

name: Rabo-de-Galo
description: 'Rooster's tail': cachaça and red vermouth, stirred and served short. Brazil's Manhattan, drunk standing up at a botequim counter.
funFact: The name is a literal translation of 'cocktail'; the traditional street version is a rough 50/50 of cachaça and Cynar, while the bar version leans on aged cachaça and good vermouth.

steps: Combine the cachaça, vermouth and bitters in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20 seconds until chilled.
Strain into a small tumbler, over one large ice cube or straight up.
Express an orange twist over the top.

name: Borgoña
description: Red wine and macerated strawberries, chilled and eaten as much as drunk. Chile's Fiestas Patrias in a jug.
funFact: Served at every September 18 fonda alongside its white-wine cousin, the chicha-based Clery; the strawberries at the bottom of the jug are the prize and go to whoever is quickest.

steps: Toss the strawberries with the sugar in a large jug and leave for an hour to macerate.
Pour over the red wine and stir.
Refrigerate for at least two hours — overnight is better.
Serve cold over ice, spooning strawberries into each glass.

name: Cola de Mono
description: 'Monkey's tail': coffee, milk, cloves and aguardiente, chilled and bottled for Christmas. Chile's answer to eggnog, and considerably more drinkable.
funFact: Chilean families bottle it in reused wine bottles in early December and keep it in the fridge until Christmas Eve; the name's origin is disputed, with the best story involving President Pedro Montt and a borrowed pistol.

steps: Warm the milk with the sugar, cloves and cinnamon until the sugar dissolves; do not boil.
Stir in the instant coffee and vanilla, then remove from the heat.
Cool completely and strain out the spices.
Stir in the aguardiente, bottle, and refrigerate for at least a day.
Serve very cold in small glasses.

name: Piscola
description: Pisco and cola, no ceremony. Chile's default drink at every party, poured with a heavy hand and measured by nobody.
funFact: Chile consumes so much of it that pisco producers bottle expressly for the mix; there is an annual National Piscola Day, and the drink is often blamed for Chile's reputation as South America's heaviest spirit drinkers.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the pisco.
Top with cold cola.
Stir once. Add a lime wedge only if you must — most Chileans do not.

name: Serena Libre
description: Pisco with papaya juice and a squeeze of lime — the northern Chilean coast's alternative to the Piscola, built on the fruit that grows there.
funFact: The papaya of La Serena is a small, aromatic variety grown in the Elqui Valley — the same valley that produces most of Chile's pisco, which is why the pairing is local rather than clever.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the pisco, papaya juice and lime juice.
Stir well to combine.
Top with a splash of soda and garnish with a lime wheel.

name: Guaro Sour Colombiano
description: Aguardiente antioqueño — anise-forward and unapologetic — shaken with lime and sugar into something that tames it, slightly.
funFact: Colombian aguardiente is flavoured with anise, which makes it a completely different animal from Costa Rican guaro; the sin azúcar version now outsells the sweetened original.

steps: Dry-shake the aguardiente, lime, syrup and egg white without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard again for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lime twist across the foam.

name: Refajo
description: Beer and Colombiana cream soda, poured half and half. Sweet, fizzy, faintly ridiculous, and served at every Colombian family lunch.
funFact: Colombiana is a red 'kola champagne' soda bottled since 1904; the mix has been formalised into a canned product, but Colombians still insist the fresh pour is better.

steps: Chill both the beer and the soda thoroughly.
Pour equal parts into a tall glass, soda first to control the foam.
Stir once, very gently.
For a 'refajo con aguardiente', add a shot of aguardiente before topping up.

name: Canelazo
description: Andean altitude medicine: cinnamon and naranjilla simmered with sugar, spiked with aguardiente and drunk hot at ten thousand feet.
funFact: Naranjilla — lulo in Colombia — is a small orange Andean fruit that tastes like rhubarb crossed with citrus, and it is what separates a real canelazo from hot cinnamon water with booze in it.

steps: Simmer the water with the cinnamon sticks and panela for 15 minutes.
Add the naranjilla pulp and lime juice and simmer for another 5 minutes.
Strain into mugs.
Add the aguardiente to each mug off the heat.
Serve immediately with a cinnamon stick.

name: Caña con Ruda
description: Cane spirit steeped with rue, drunk in one shot on the first of August. Bitter, herbal and, by tradition, obligatory.
funFact: Guaraní tradition holds that a shot of caña con ruda on an empty stomach on August 1 wards off the illnesses of the coming winter; the custom is shared with Argentina and Uruguay.

steps: Wash and dry the rue sprig thoroughly.
Push it into the bottle of caña and seal.
Leave to macerate for at least a week — traditionally from the previous winter.
On the morning of August 1, pour a single shot and drink it on an empty stomach.
Do not drink more than three: the tradition is specific about this.

name: Clericó
description: White wine and chopped summer fruit, chilled hard. Sangria's lighter South American cousin, and Christmas dinner across the Southern Cone.
funFact: Because Christmas falls in high summer in Paraguay, the festive drink is served ice cold with fruit — the name traces back to the English 'claret cup' by way of Spanish.

ingredients.item: Mixed fruit (peach, apple, orange, grape), diced

steps: Toss the diced fruit with the sugar and leave for an hour.
Pour over the white wine and refrigerate for at least four hours.
Top with soda water just before serving.
Serve very cold, spooning plenty of fruit into each glass.

name: Algarrobina
description: Pisco with carob syrup, condensed milk and egg — dark, sweet and faintly smoky, Peru's dessert cocktail and reputed aphrodisiac.
funFact: Algarrobina is boiled down from the pods of the Peruvian carob tree that grows in the northern deserts; Peruvians credit it, without much evidence and with great confidence, with restorative powers.

steps: Add the pisco, algarrobina, condensed milk and egg yolk to a blender.
Add the ice and blend until thick and uniform.
Pour into a chilled coupe.
Drizzle a little extra algarrobina over the surface and dust with cinnamon.

name: Capitán
description: The Peruvian Manhattan: pisco and red vermouth, stirred cold. Sipped in the highlands where the nights get serious.
funFact: It belongs to Puno and the Peruvian Andes, where army officers — the 'capitanes' of the name — are credited with the habit of cutting pisco with vermouth against the cold.

steps: Add the pisco, vermouth and bitters to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20 to 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry or a lemon twist.

name: Chilcano
description: Peru's everyday pisco drink: pisco, ginger ale, lime and bitters over ice. Lighter than a Pisco Sour and far easier to make ten of.
funFact: Peru holds a national Semana del Chilcano every January; the drink descends from the 'chilcano de pescado', a fish broth once drunk as a hangover cure in the port of Chilca.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the pisco and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger ale.
Dash the Angostura over the surface.
Stir once gently and garnish with a lime wheel.

name: Machu Picchu
description: Green, yellow and red in one tall glass, layered to look like the mountain at sunrise. A tourist drink Cusco has fully embraced.
funFact: It exists almost entirely for the photograph — but Cusco's bars have made it well enough for long enough that it has become a genuine local order.

steps: Pour the grenadine into the bottom of a tall glass.
Fill the glass carefully with crushed ice to hold the layers apart.
Shake the pisco with the orange juice and pour slowly over the ice.
Float the crème de menthe on top over the back of a spoon.
Serve with a straw and let the drinker mix it themselves.

name: Medio y Medio
description: Half sparkling wine, half sweet white — Uruguay's national aperitif, poured at the Mercado del Puerto beside a plate of grilled meat.
funFact: The Roldós stall in Montevideo's Mercado del Puerto has been mixing it since 1886 and bottles its own; the ratio is exactly what the name says, and nobody there will negotiate.

steps: Chill both wines thoroughly.
Pour the sweet white wine into a wine glass first.
Top with the sparkling wine, poured slowly down the side to preserve the bubbles.
Serve immediately, without ice.

name: Guarapita
description: Rum or aguardiente loaded with passionfruit and sugar, mixed in a jug and served from a plastic bottle at the beach. Deceptively fruity.
funFact: Guarapita is Venezuelan beach and street-party currency, usually sold in recycled water bottles — the fruit hides the proof so effectively that it is known as 'the liar'.

steps: Stir the sugar into the passionfruit and orange juice until fully dissolved.
Add the rum and mix well.
Chill for at least two hours.
Serve very cold over ice, and warn people.

name: Ponche Crema
description: Venezuela's Christmas cream: eggs, milk, sugar and rum cooked into a custard-thick liqueur that coats the glass and the season.
funFact: Eliodoro González P. commercialised it in 1900 and the brand still dominates December in Venezuela, but home-made versions with a heavier rum hand remain the point of pride.

steps: Whisk the egg yolks with the condensed milk over a very low heat until slightly thickened; do not let it scramble.
Remove from the heat and whisk in the evaporated milk and vanilla.
Cool completely to room temperature.
Stir in the rum, then bottle and refrigerate overnight.
Serve chilled with nutmeg grated over the top.
